To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the current source density (i.e., the current per unit area in the extracellular space) is not zero in barrel cortex, and (ii) the current source monopole hypothesis (i.e., that current monopoles exist on a mesoscopic scale) is incorrect.
the estimated instantaneous CSD from extracellular potentials does NOT sum to zero over a barrel column in anesthetized rats, and that the estimated CSD does not obey Ohm’s Law.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of new methods for analyzing and interpreting multichannel electrophysiology recordings from the brain, with the aim of understanding the underlying mechanisms of information processing.
the design and synthesis of a new class of compounds, the so-called "monopoles", and with their possible applications as molecular magnets.
the development and implementation of a novel approach for the analysis of multielectrodic signals in the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
current monopoles do not exist in the brain, and that the estimated current source monopole in the study by Riera et al (2012) is a numerical artifact.
the presence of a current monopole in a macroscopic system (e.g., a cortical column) is impossible.
, while the presence of current monopole sources is not ruled out, it is not possible to conclude that they are present in the data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the current density Jf must be divergence-free (i.e., a curl).
the current density Jf must sum to zero at all times and all points in the brain.
the neuronal current-source density is a macroscopic quantity, which is not equal to the microscopic current density of free charge carriers.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the traditional cable theory of neurons is still a valid model for neuronal electrophysiology and, therefore, that the current monopoles estimated in the barrel cortex are artifacts of the CSD estimation method.
the current source monopole concept is not a valid description of neuronal activity.
the traditional interpretation of extracellular potentials as the superposition of a large number of current dipoles (the cable equation) is not sufficient for explaining multielectrodes data.
